title: Ellipsis & substitution
note: verb-phrase ellipsis and the stranded auxiliary (including do-support and the to of want/need) · so / neither / nor with obligatory inversion, and either without it · nominal substitution across one, ones, another, the other, others, the others, the same · clausal so and not after think, hope, suppose, say, be afraid and if, plus do so · 4 strands x 12 · 48 items · built to live 2026-08-07 (cloud run 14)

cards.title: Say it once
cards.body: English has two ways of not repeating itself. Ellipsis deletes the repeated words and leaves a hole the reader fills from the previous clause. Substitution puts a small stand-in word where they were. Both are obligatory in good English — repeating the full phrase is not neutral, it is heavy — and both are places where a Czech sentence would simply carry on.
cards.body_cz: Angličtina má dva způsoby, jak se neopakovat. Elipsa opakovaná slova vypustí a nechá mezeru, kterou si čtenář doplní z předchozí věty. Substituce na jejich místo dosadí krátké zástupné slovo. Obojí je v dobré angličtině povinné — zopakovat celou frázi není neutrální, nýbrž těžkopádné — a v obou případech by česká věta prostě pokračovala dál.

table.caption: the two mechanisms
rows: He said he would call, but he didn't call.
She can swim better than I can swim.
I would like the big room.
I would like the big one.
I hope you are coming this evening.

cards.title: The auxiliary stays behind
cards.body: In verb-phrase ellipsis the auxiliary or the modal survives and everything after it goes. If the first clause has no auxiliary of its own, do appears to be the survivor. The word left standing agrees with its own subject and carries its own tense — it is not a copy of the clause it replaces.
cards.body_cz: Při elipse slovesné fráze přežije pomocné či způsobové sloveso a vše za ním zmizí. Nemá-li první věta vlastní pomocné sloveso, objeví se jako přeživší do. Slovo, které zůstane stát, se shoduje se svým vlastním podmětem a nese vlastní čas — není kopií věty, kterou zastupuje.
points: No auxiliary in the first clause? do steps in: She works hard → than he does.
After want, need, try and like the survivor is to, not do: if you want to.
Tense is chosen fresh: I thought she was ready, but she wasn't — not isn't.

cards.title: so and neither invert
cards.body: To add a second subject to the same statement, English puts so or neither first, then the auxiliary, then the subject. The inversion is not optional and it is the half Czech speakers leave out, because taky and taky ne do the whole job on their own.
cards.body_cz: Chce-li angličtina k témuž tvrzení připojit další podmět, postaví dopředu so nebo neither, pak pomocné sloveso a teprve pak podmět. Inverze není volitelná a právě ji čeští mluvčí vypouštějí, protože taky a taky ne celou práci zastanou samy.
points: Positive → so. Negative → neither or nor. Both invert: so does she, not so she does.
either does the same work without inverting, and goes at the end.
neither and nor are already negative — never add n't to the verb after them.

cards.title: one and ones
cards.body: A countable noun already named is replaced by one, or by ones in the plural. Czech drops the noun and leaves the adjective standing alone, which is exactly what English will not do: the big is not a noun phrase, the big one is.
cards.body_cz: Počitatelné jméno, které už zaznělo, se nahrazuje slovem one, v množném čísle ones. Čeština jméno vypustí a nechá stát samotné přídavné jméno — a právě to angličtina nepřipouští: the big není jmenná fráze, the big one ano.

table.caption: dividing a set
rows: I would like the big one.
one more of the same kind
all the rest of a known set

points: one is obligatory after an adjective: the first one, not the first.
one replaces countable nouns only — never water, money or work.
another is one word and always singular.

cards.title: so and not for a whole clause
cards.title_cz: so a not za celou větu
cards.body: After a small fixed set of verbs, so stands in for an entire clause and not is its negative. The list is short — think, hope, suppose, say, be afraid — and it does not extend to know or see, where English uses it or nothing at all.
cards.body_cz: Po malé, pevně dané skupině sloves zastupuje so celou větu a not je jeho záporem. Seznam je krátký — think, hope, suppose, say, be afraid — a nepatří do něj know ani see, kde angličtina užívá it nebo vůbec nic.
points: think moves the negative onto the verb; hope and be afraid keep it on not.
if so and if not carry a whole condition: Is the shop open? If so, we can go now.
do so replaces an action already described and belongs to writing; speech prefers do it.
The contracted forms are equally correct and are accepted: I'm afraid so, I don't think so.

cards.title: When not to leave it out
cards.body: Ellipsis only works when the reader can rebuild the missing words exactly, from the clause immediately before. If two possible antecedents are in play, or the tense or the subject has shifted in a way the surviving word does not show, write the phrase out. Silence is only economical while it is unambiguous.
cards.body_cz: Elipsa funguje jen tehdy, dokáže-li si čtenář chybějící slova přesně doplnit z bezprostředně předcházející věty. Jsou-li ve hře dva možní odkazovaní členové nebo posunul-li se čas či podmět způsobem, který přeživší slovo neukáže, napište frázi celou. Vypuštění je úsporné jen do chvíle, kdy je jednoznačné.

table.caption: keep it, or lose the reader
rows: Petr told Jan he would, but he didn't.
two men, two he — rebuild it and say which
two different verb phrases are in play
The report is ready and the letters too.
singular verb cannot cover a plural subject

points: Rebuild the full sentence in your head; if it comes back the same, the ellipsis is safe.
Across a paragraph break, write it out — the antecedent is too far away.
In formal writing the full phrase is never wrong, only heavier.

items.en: He said he would call, but he didn't.
items.cz: Řekl, že zavolá, ale nezavolal.
items.gap: He said he would call, but he ____.
accepts: He said he would call, but he didn't.
items.explanation: English does not repeat a verb phrase it has already used. It leaves the auxiliary or the modal standing alone and deletes everything after it, so he said he would call, but he didn't ends where a Czech sentence would carry on. If there is no auxiliary in the first clause, do steps in to be the one left behind. The stranded word still carries tense and number, which is why it has to be chosen and not guessed: it agrees with its own subject, not with the clause it is standing in for.
items.explanation_cz: Angličtina neopakuje slovesnou frázi, kterou už jednou použila. Nechá stát samotné pomocné či způsobové sloveso a všechno za ním vypustí, takže he said he would call, but he didn't končí tam, kde by česká věta pokračovala. Nemá-li první věta pomocné sloveso, nastoupí místo něj do. Osamocené slovo přitom pořád nese čas i číslo, a proto se musí volit, ne hádat: shoduje se se svým vlastním podmětem, nikoli s větou, kterou zastupuje.

items.en: I like coffee and so does she.
items.cz: Mám rád kávu a ona taky.
items.gap: I like coffee and ____ does she.
accepts: I like coffee and so does she.
items.explanation: To say that the same thing is true of someone else, English inverts: so or neither, then the auxiliary, then the subject — so does she, neither have we. The inversion is obligatory and it is the part Czech speakers drop, because Czech manages the whole job with taky and taky ne. Polarity picks the word: so after a positive clause, neither or nor after a negative one. Either does the same work but keeps normal word order and goes at the end: I can't either.
items.explanation_cz: Chce-li angličtina říct, že totéž platí i o někom jiném, obrátí pořádek slov: so nebo neither, pak pomocné sloveso, pak podmět — so does she, neither have we. Inverze je povinná a právě ji čeští mluvčí vynechávají, protože čeština si vystačí s taky a taky ne. Slovo vybírá kladnost či zápornost věty: so po kladné, neither nebo nor po záporné. Either dělá totéž, ale zachovává běžný slovosled a stojí na konci: I can't either.

Either dělá totéž, ale zachovává běžný slovosled a stojí na konci: I can't either.

items.explanation: To say that the same thing is true of someone else, English inverts: so or neither, then the auxiliary, then the subject — so does she, neither have we. The inversion is obligatory and it is the part Czech speakers drop, because Czech manages the whole job with taky and taky ne. Polarity picks the word: so after a positive clause, neither or nor after a negative one. Either does the same work but keeps normal word order and goes at the end: I can't either.

items.en: There are two rooms. I would like the big one.

items.explanation: A noun that has already been named is replaced, not repeated: one for a singular countable noun, ones for a plural. Czech simply drops the noun and lets the adjective stand alone — ten velký — which is why Czech speakers write I would like the big and hear nothing wrong with it. One is obligatory after an adjective. Around it sits a small family that divides a set up: another for one more of the same, the other for the remaining one, others and the others for the rest.
items.explanation_cz: Podstatné jméno, které už zaznělo, se nahrazuje, neopakuje: one u počitatelného jména v jednotném čísle, ones v množném. Čeština jméno prostě vypustí a nechá stát samotné přídavné jméno — ten velký — a proto čeští mluvčí píšou I would like the big a nic jim na tom nezní špatně. Po přídavném jménu je one povinné. Kolem něj stojí malá rodina slov, která dělí množinu: another pro další stejný kus, the other pro ten zbývající, others a the others pro zbytek.

items.explanation_cz: Podstatné jméno, které už zaznělo, se nahrazuje, neopakuje: one u počitatelného jména v jednotném čísle, ones v množném. Čeština jméno prostě vypustí a nechá stát samotné přídavné jméno — ten velký — a proto čeští mluvčí píšou I would like the big a nic jim na tom nezní špatně. Po přídavném jménu je one povinné. Kolem něj stojí malá rodina slov, která dělí množinu: another pro další stejný kus, the other pro ten zbývající, others a the others pro zbytek.
